name: Feasts, Festivals, and the Jewish Calendar

objectives.text: Identify Passover as the meal God commanded Israel to eat to remember how He rescued them from Egypt
Retell that God gave Israel a weekly day of rest called the Sabbath
Recall that God commanded Israel's feasts so His people would remember His works and give thanks to Him
Describe how Israelites lived in booths during the Feast of Tabernacles and tell what the booths helped them remember
Describe how Jesus traveled with His family to Jerusalem to keep the Passover as a boy
Identify Hanukkah as the Feast of Dedication that celebrated the rededication of the temple and recall that Jesus was in the temple during this feast
Summarize the parts of the first Passover, including the lamb, the blood on the doorposts, the unleavened bread, and the bitter herbs, and explain what each recalled
Explain why the Jews celebrate Purim using the account in the book of Esther
Identify the three pilgrimage feasts and explain why Israelites traveled to Jerusalem to keep them
Explain the Feast of Weeks as a harvest festival of firstfruits held fifty days after the Passover season
Compare the weekly Sabbath with Israel's yearly festivals in purpose and practice
Describe how the Jewish calendar follows the moon, beginning each month at the new moon and the religious year in the spring month of Abib or Nisan
Explain the rituals of the Day of Atonement, including the high priest entering the Most Holy Place and the sending away of the scapegoat
Describe the commands for the Feast of Firstfruits and the Feast of Trumpets
Construct a calendar of Israel's appointed feasts showing their months, agricultural seasons, and the events of redemption each recalled
Explain the sabbatical year and the Year of Jubilee and how Jesus applied jubilee language to His ministry
Explain how Hanukkah arose from the Maccabean revolt against Antiochus IV, treating 1 Maccabees as a useful historical source that is not inspired Scripture
Interpret Jesus as the fulfillment of the Passover by connecting the Last Supper and the apostolic teaching that Christ is our Passover lamb
Analyze how the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost connects to the Feast of Weeks as a firstfruits harvest
Analyze how Jesus used the water and light imagery of the Feast of Tabernacles to reveal who He is
Analyze how Hebrews presents Christ's priestly work as the fulfillment of the Day of Atonement
Compare the feast commands of the Torah with practices that developed by the Second Temple period, such as Passover Seder customs and the water-pouring rite at Tabernacles
Explain the Reformed teaching that Israel's feasts belonged to the ceremonial law, foreshadowed Christ, and are now fulfilled and abrogated
Explain how the Reformed tradition understands the Lord's Supper in relation to the Passover and the Lord's Day in relation to the Sabbath
Evaluate interpretations of feast typology by distinguishing types the New Testament itself establishes from speculative prophetic schemes
Evaluate arguments about whether Christians are bound to keep the Jewish feasts using Paul's teaching and the Reformed confession on Christian liberty
Create a presentation or essay tracing how Israel's cycle of feasts retells the history of redemption and points to its completion in the new creation

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (Passover, Hanukkah, purpose of feasts, Seder/first Passover, Weeks, Sabbath vs festivals, Tabernacles, Day of Atonement, calendar construction, Maccabean context, Passover and Pentecost fulfillment, typology, cycle of remembrance). Dropped 'Observe a Menorah' as not assessable and folded 'prophetic meaning' into a grounded typology evaluation. Added Purim, pilgrimage feasts, lunar calendar, Firstfruits and Trumpets, Jubilee, Jesus at feasts in Luke and John, Second Temple developments, Hebrews on Atonement, Reformed teaching on ceremonial law, Lord's Supper and Lord's Day, and Christian liberty. Replaced whole-chapter references with verse ranges and added confessional anchors only where they state the doctrine.
